title: The greeting to the dead
hookLine: peace upon you, people of these dwellings (Muslim)
carry: peace upon you, people of the graves

lines: WHAT SHOULD I SAY TO THEM?
cards: It's night in Madinah, and 'A'ishah is awake when her husband gets up.
In a long hadith in Sahih Muslim, she tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, slipped out quietly, and she followed him through the dark to al-Baqi', the graveyard.
He stood there a long time, raised his hands three times, and turned back. She hurried home ahead of him, out of breath, and he asked what was wrong. It all came out.
Then she asked the question underneath it: what should I say to them, when I go there?

teach.b: He told her. And in another report in Sahih Muslim, from Buraydah, he taught the same words to his companions when they went out to the graves. They begin: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar.
Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then, in paraphrase: you who are believers and Muslims, and we, if God wills, will be joining you. And it asks God for well-being, for us and for you.

teach.h: THE SAME GREETING AS THE LIVING.
teach.b: As-salamu 'alaykum is the greeting Muslims give the living: at the door, in the street, at the close of the prayer. Here it's said to the dead, in the same words, the way you'd greet a neighbor.
And the graves are called dwellings. Homes. The people buried there are residents, and you're a visitor in their neighborhood.
Then the honest middle line: we will be joining you. Nobody pretends otherwise. The visitor and the visited are on the same road, at different points along it.
The last line asks well-being for both at once. The living don't stand above the dead, praying down at them; they stand beside them and ask together.
In 'A'ishah's version the Prophet also asks mercy for those who have gone ahead and those who come later. One greeting, and the whole line of people, before and after, is inside it.

how: When Muslims enter a graveyard, they greet the dead with the words the Prophet taught, beginning "as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar", and ask God's well-being and mercy for those buried there and for themselves.

games.q: what does “the greeting to the dead” mean?
o: the Prophet's words of peace for those in their graves
a prayer the imam leads before the body is buried
the last words a dying person is helped to say

games.q: the greeting to the dead — tap the pairs.
p: asked what should I say to them?
the graveyard he went to at night
the greeting taught to the companions

s: the dead are greeted with a special phrase used nowhere else
it opens with as-salamu 'alaykum, the greeting given to the living.
the greeting says the living will be joining the dead
we, if God wills, will be joining you.
the greeting asks well-being only for the dead
it asks for us and for you.

games.q: you're 'A'ishah. you followed the Prophet to the graveyard at night, and now it's all come out. what do you ask him?
o: why did you leave without telling me?
what should I say to them, when I go?
games.why: in Sahih Muslim she asks what she should say to them, and he teaches her the greeting.

practice: Say the opening quietly a few times, until it sits easily: as-salamu 'alaykum, ahl ad-diyar, peace be upon you, people of these dwellings. Then think of a graveyard you know and the people resting there, named or unnamed.
If you pray, you can offer them the greeting as it was taught; if not, simply hold them in mind as neighbors on the same road.

wordCard.voice: The greeting to the dead. Peace be upon you, people of these dwellings: the Prophet's words for greeting those in their graves. Today's word.
